Twelve stages take you from an empty laptop to publication-style figures. You will install the tools, learn pandas on a tiny table, build a project folder, then audit and plot a real dataset of more than four thousand protein variants. No biology is needed: every column is explained when you meet it.

  • Run it yourself.Each stage ends with a puzzle. Do the work on your own machine and type the answer you get.
  • Earn two stars a stage.The first star unlocks a harder second one. Twenty-four in all, about ten hours in total.
  • Nothing leaves your browser.Progress is saved in this browser only. Nothing is uploaded and there is no account.

Stage 0

Basecamp: set up your tools

★★

By the end you will have an isolated Python environment, an editor that understands it, and proof that both talk to each other. About 40 minutes.

Most beginner pain is not about Python at all. It is about which Python is running, and where. So we fix that first, once, properly.

1. Install VS Code

Download it from code.visualstudio.com and run the installer. VS Code is a text editor that grows into an IDE when you add extensions. It will be where you write scripts, run notebooks, browse files, and use a terminal, all in one window.

macOS only: enable the code command

Open VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+P, type Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH and press Enter. Windows and Linux installers usually do this for you.

2. Install Miniconda from the command line

conda is a program that creates environments: separate folders, each with its own Python and its own set of libraries. Project A can use pandas 2 while project B uses pandas 3, and neither can break the other. Miniconda is the small installer: just conda and Python. We install it entirely from the terminal. Open a terminal first: Terminal on macOS or Linux, PowerShell on Windows (Start menu, type PowerShell).

Pick your system. On a Mac, check which chip you have with uname -m: arm64 means Apple silicon, x86_64 means Intel.

macOS / Linux terminal
uname -m

# macOS, Apple silicon (arm64):
URL=https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-arm64.sh
# macOS, Intel (x86_64): use this line instead
# URL=https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-x86_64.sh
# Linux (x86_64): use this line instead
# URL=https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh

mkdir -p ~/miniconda3
curl -L $URL -o ~/miniconda3/miniconda.sh
bash ~/miniconda3/miniconda.sh -b -u -p ~/miniconda3
rm ~/miniconda3/miniconda.sh

~/miniconda3/bin/conda init bash zsh
Windows (PowerShell)
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Windows-x86_64.exe" -OutFile ".\miniconda.exe"
Start-Process -FilePath ".\miniconda.exe" -ArgumentList "/InstallationType=JustMe","/RegisterPython=0","/S","/D=$env:USERPROFILE\miniconda3" -Wait
Remove-Item ".\miniconda.exe"

& "$env:USERPROFILE\miniconda3\Scripts\conda.exe" init powershell

The last line connects conda to your shell. Close the terminal completely and open a new one. The prompt should now start with (base). Then check:

terminal
conda --version
which python    # Windows: Get-Command python
Windows: "running scripts is disabled on this system"

PowerShell blocks the startup file conda adds. Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, answer Y, then open a new PowerShell window.

conda says something about "Terms of Service"

Newer conda versions can stop and ask you to accept channel terms before installing packages. The message prints the exact command to run. Copy it, run it, then repeat your original command. This is your first lesson in reading error messages: the answer was in the message.

Optional but pleasant: stop conda from activating base in every new terminal.

terminal
conda config --set auto_activate_base false

3. Create the environment

One command makes a fresh environment called pandas-quest with everything this guide needs:

terminal
conda create -n pandas-quest -c conda-forge python=3.12 pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn scipy ipykernel -y

Then step inside it. You will do this every time you open a new terminal:

terminal
conda activate pandas-quest

Your prompt now starts with (pandas-quest). That prefix is your seatbelt light: if it is missing, you are not in the environment.

4. Make a project folder and open it

macOS / Linux terminal
mkdir pandas-quest
cd pandas-quest
code .
Windows (Anaconda Prompt)
mkdir pandas-quest
cd pandas-quest
code .

VS Code opens with that folder. Always open the folder, not single files. It is what lets VS Code find your data, scripts and environment.

5. Add extensions

Open the Extensions panel (Ctrl+Shift+X, or Cmd+Shift+X on Mac) and search by name, or paste these in the terminal:

terminal
code --install-extension ms-python.python
code --install-extension ms-toolsai.jupyter
code --install-extension mechatroner.rainbow-csv
code --install-extension ms-toolsai.datawrangler
code --install-extension usernamehw.errorlens
ExtensionWhat it does for you
PythonRuns and debugs .py files, finds your conda environments, adds autocomplete.
JupyterOpens .ipynb notebooks inside VS Code and runs cells.
Rainbow CSVColours each column of a CSV differently so you can read raw data files.
Data WranglerOpens a DataFrame as a scrollable grid with summary stats.
Error LensPrints errors and warnings at the end of the offending line. Great for making errors feel normal.

6. Tell VS Code which Python to use

Press Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P, type Python: Select Interpreter, and choose the one named pandas-quest. Its path contains envs/pandas-quest. A notebook has its own picker, which you will use in the next stage.

7. Run the check script

In VS Code create a new file named check_setup.py (File, New File), paste this in, save, and run it from the terminal with python check_setup.py.

check_setup.py
import sys
import platform

print("python    ", platform.python_version())
for name in ["pandas", "numpy", "matplotlib", "seaborn", "scipy"]:
    module = __import__(name)
    print(f"{name:<10}", module.__version__)
print("env       ", sys.prefix.replace("\\", "/").split("/")[-1])

You should see something shaped like this (your version numbers will differ):

example output
python     3.12.8
pandas     3.0.1
numpy      2.3.5
matplotlib 3.10.7
seaborn    0.13.2
scipy      1.16.3
env        pandas-quest
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'

Python is running, but it is not the one inside pandas-quest. Check for the (pandas-quest) prefix in your terminal, and re-run Python: Select Interpreter. Nine times out of ten, this is the whole story.

★

First star

Paste everything check_setup.py printed. The checker looks for Python, pandas, matplotlib and seaborn versions, and an env line that says pandas-quest.

Stuck? Nudge and solution

If a library line is missing, the install command in step 3 did not finish. Run it again and read the last lines it prints.

★

Second star

Now prove VS Code itself uses that environment. In the next stage you will create a notebook; for now, any notebook will do (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P, then Create: New Jupyter Notebook). Click Select Kernel at the top right, pick pandas-quest, run this in a cell, and paste the path it prints.

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Not seeing pandas-quest in the kernel list? Click the refresh icon in the kernel picker, or restart VS Code once. The environment needs ipykernel installed, which step 3 did.

one way to get it
import sys
print(sys.executable)
Stage 1

Notebook Ridge: cells, kernels and Python basics

★★

You will learn the one rule that explains most notebook weirdness, then use strings, loops and conditions to take a variant name apart. About 50 minutes.

A Jupyter notebook (.ipynb) mixes code, results and notes in one document. It is made of cells. Code cells run Python and show what they produce underneath. Markdown cells hold text, headings and reminders to future you.

Keyboard shortcuts worth learning today
  • Shift+Enter: run the cell and move to the next one.
  • Esc, then A or B: insert a cell above or below.
  • Esc, then M or Y: turn a cell into Markdown or code.
  • Esc, then D D: delete the cell.

Create notebooks/01_python_basics.ipynb in your project (make the notebooks folder if it does not exist), select the pandas-quest kernel, and follow along cell by cell.

The kernel is a running program with a memory

Behind the notebook is a kernel: a Python process that executes your cells and remembers every variable you have created. The notebook shows the code; the kernel holds the state. They can disagree. Try it:

cell 1
x = 10
cell 2
print(x * 2)

Run both: you get 20. Now edit cell 1 to x = 100 but do not run it, then re-run cell 2. Still 20. The page says 100; the kernel still thinks 10.

The notebook rule

A notebook is only trustworthy if it works from the top, in order, in a fresh kernel. Get in the habit of using Restart then Run All (toolbar buttons) before you believe any result, and before you share a notebook.

Printing, and what shows up on its own

The last expression in a cell is displayed automatically. print() is for everything else: checking an assumption, logging progress inside a loop, leaving yourself a trail of what happened. F-strings make labels painless:

cell
n_reads = 1250
print(f"reads counted: {n_reads}")
print(f"as thousands: {n_reads / 1000:.2f}k")
When to print

Print while you are figuring things out; delete or reduce the prints once you trust a step. Loud notebooks hide the one line that matters.

Data types, in five lines

cell
count = 24             # int
score = 3.49           # float
name = "p.Trp18Ter"    # str
is_low = score < 2     # bool
variants = ["a", "b"]  # list
print(type(count), type(score), type(name), type(is_low), type(variants))

type(x) is the first thing to check when something behaves strangely. It is the notebook equivalent of looking at the label on the jar.

Strings, and slicing them

A slice text[start:stop] takes characters from start up to, but not including, stop. Counting starts at 0, and negative numbers count from the end.

cell
v = "p.Trp18Ter"
#    index: 0123456789...
print(v[2:5])    # Trp
print(v[5:-3])   # 18
print(v[-3:])    # Ter
print(int(v[5:-3]) + 1)   # 19
print(v.startswith("p."), v.endswith("Ter"), v.upper(), v.replace("p.", ""))
Off-by-one

v[2:5] has three characters, not four, because the stop position is excluded. When a slice is wrong by one, write out the indices on paper. It takes ten seconds.

Math, conditions, loops

cell
print(7 + 2, 7 - 2, 7 * 2, 7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 7 ** 2)   # 9 5 14 3.5 3 1 49
print(round(3.4902, 2))
cell
score = 1.4
if score < 0.5:
    label = "low"
elif score < 1.0:
    label = "in between"
else:
    label = "wild-type-like"
print(label)
cell
names = ["WT", "p.Trp18Ter", "p.Leu25Pro"]
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(i, name, len(name))

# the same idea in one line, called a list comprehension
lengths = [len(name) for name in names]

Python reads close to English: for each name in names, print it. Indentation (four spaces) is how Python knows what is inside the loop or the if, so it is part of the grammar, not decoration.

Here is the list you will use for the puzzles. Every entry follows the pattern p. + three-letter reference + position + three-letter alternate. (Ter means the sequence stops there; the same three letters twice means nothing changed.)

cell
variants = ["p.Gly12Gly", "p.Trp18Ter", "p.Leu25Pro", "p.Val30Asp",
            "p.Gln36Ter", "p.Ile40Asn", "p.Ser45Thr", "p.Gly46Arg"]
★

First star

Using slicing, pull the position number out of every variant, convert it to an integer, and add them all up. What is the sum?

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Every variant has the same shape, so v[5:-3] works for all of them. Loop over the list and add int(...) to a running total starting at 0.

one way to get it
total = 0
for v in variants:
    total += int(v[5:-3])
print(total)
★

Second star

Classify each variant with a loop and if/elif/else: synonymous if the reference and alternate letters are identical, nonsense if the alternate is Ter, otherwise missense. Report the counts in the order synonymous, nonsense, missense, separated by commas.

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Reference is v[2:5] and alternate is v[-3:]. Check synonymous first, then nonsense. Keep three counters and print them with an f-string.

one way to get it
syn = non = mis = 0
for v in variants:
    ref, alt = v[2:5], v[-3:]
    if ref == alt:
        syn += 1
    elif alt == "Ter":
        non += 1
    else:
        mis += 1
print(f"{syn},{non},{mis}")
Stage 2

Traceback Gorge: errors are directions, not insults

★★

Every programmer sees red text all day. The skill is not avoiding it, it is reading it fast. You will learn the anatomy of an error and a repeatable way to chase one down. About 35 minutes.

An error message is the computer telling you, as precisely as it can, where it got stuck and why. It is more helpful than most feedback you will ever get. Here is a real one from a notebook:

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
KeyError                                  Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[4], line 2
      1 df = pd.read_csv("data/raw/toy.csv")
----> 2 print(df["Score"].mean())

File ~/miniconda3/envs/pandas-quest/lib/python3.12/site-packages/pandas/core/frame.py:4102, in DataFrame.__getitem__(self, key)
   ... (about thirty lines of pandas internals) ...

KeyError: 'Score'
  1. Start at the bottom. KeyError: 'Score' says: you asked for something by name and it is not there. The type tells you the category; the message tells you the specifics.
  2. Find your line. The arrow ----> 2 points at your code. Ignore the middle section about library internals; those are the pandas authors' lines, and the bug is almost never theirs.
  3. Ask what you would expect. Which column names really exist? print(df.columns). You will see score, lowercase. Keys are case-sensitive.

The usual suspects

ErrorPlain-English meaningFirst thing to try
SyntaxErrorPython could not even read the code. A missing colon, quote or bracket. Nothing ran.Look at the line it marks and the line above.
NameErrorYou used a name Python has never seen.Typo? Or you did not run the cell that creates it (kernel memory!).
TypeErrorRight operation, wrong kind of thing, such as adding a string to a number.print(type(x)) for each thing involved.
ValueErrorRight kind of thing, unacceptable value, such as int("abc").Print the value that was passed in.
KeyErrorA dictionary key or DataFrame column is not there.df.columns. Check case and stray spaces.
IndexErrorYou asked for item 10 of a list with 5 items.len(...) before indexing.
AttributeErrorThat object has no such method or attribute.Typo, or it is a different type than you think.
FileNotFoundErrorThe path points to nothing.Print the current folder with from pathlib import Path; Path.cwd().
ModuleNotFoundErrorThe library is not installed in this environment.Wrong kernel or interpreter. Stage 0, step 6.

A routine that works

  1. Read the last line of the traceback out loud, slowly.
  2. Go to the line the arrow points at. Is it what you expected to run?
  3. Check what you assumed: print(type(x)), df.shape, df.columns, df.head().
  4. Shrink the problem. Reproduce it on three rows, or in a fresh cell with two lines.
  5. Suspect the kernel. Restart and Run All. A surprising number of bugs vanish.
  6. Search the message with your own names removed: KeyError pandas column beats KeyError 'Score'. Read the answer for why it happens, not just a line to copy.
  7. Still stuck? Write a question someone can answer: what you wanted, what you ran, the full error, what you already tried. That is also the best prompt for an AI assistant, which is a fine tool as long as you understand the fix before pasting it in.
Loud failures are a gift

The dangerous bugs do not raise errors at all. They give you a plausible, wrong number. This is why analysts check shapes and counts constantly, and use assert to make the computer complain on your behalf:

cell
assert len(df) == 24, f"expected 24 rows, got {len(df)}"
Errors come one at a time

Fixing one error often reveals the next. That is progress, not failure. A script with three bugs will show you three different errors, in the order Python meets them. A SyntaxError always comes first because Python reads the whole file before running a single line.

Warm-up: four quick questions about reading errors. Then a broken script to fix on your own machine.

★

First star

Pick the best answer for each.

Which line of a traceback tells you what went wrong?
KeyError: 'Score' after df["Score"]. The file's header is variant,score,se. What is the fix?
Your notebook is in notebooks/, the file is at data/raw/toy.csv, and pd.read_csv("data/raw/toy.csv") gives FileNotFoundError. Most likely cause?
total = 0, then for s in ["1.5", "2.5"]: total = total + s gives TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'. What is s?

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Question 2: the error names the key it could not find. Compare it, character by character, with the real column name.

★

Second star

This script has three separate bugs. Copy it into a new file broken.py, run it with python broken.py, and fix what the errors tell you, one at a time. When it finally runs, it prints a mean score. What is that mean, to 3 decimal places?

broken.py
scores = [3.45, 1.55, 2.18, 2.59, 3.82]

total = 0
for s in scores
    total = total + s

mean = total / len(score)
print("mean score: " + mean)

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Expect three different errors, in this order: SyntaxError (a missing character at the end of a line), then NameError (one name is misspelled), then TypeError (you cannot add a string and a float; try an f-string).

one way to get it
scores = [3.45, 1.55, 2.18, 2.59, 3.82]

total = 0
for s in scores:
    total = total + s

mean = total / len(scores)
print(f"mean score: {mean:.3f}")
Stage 3

Table Flats: your first DataFrame

★★

Libraries, read a CSV, look around, pick columns and filter rows. The four moves behind most data analysis. About 45 minutes.

A library is code someone else wrote that you borrow with import. The one that matters most here is pandas, which gives Python a table type called a DataFrame: rows are observations, columns are named measurements, and every column has a type.

Our first table is a tiny made-up experiment. No biology needed: each row is one named item measured once, and four columns (bin1_count to bin4_count) say how many reads fell into each of four buckets, from the lowest signal (bin 1) to the highest (bin 4).

Make a new notebook, notebooks/02_pandas_one.ipynb, and read the CSV straight from its web address (the file is hosted on this site):

cell
import pandas as pd

URL = "https://atharva-bhagwat.github.io/assets/data/toy_vampseq_bin_counts.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(URL)
df

Look before you touch

Before any analysis, find out what you actually have. Run each of these in its own cell:

cell
df.head()                      # first 5 rows (df.tail() for the last 5)
df.shape                       # (rows, columns)
df.columns                     # the column names
df.dtypes                      # type of each column
df.info()                      # types + missing values in one view
df.describe()                  # count, mean, min, max... of numeric columns
df["variant_type"].value_counts()   # how many rows per category
df["variant"].nunique()        # how many different variants
Types you will meet

Numbers show as int64 or float64. Text is object in pandas 2 and str in pandas 3. Both are fine. If a column that should be numeric shows up as text, something odd is hiding in it, which is worth knowing early.

Pick columns

cell
df["variant"]                       # one column -> a Series
df[["variant", "replicate"]]         # several columns -> a DataFrame (note the double brackets)

Pick rows by condition

A comparison on a column produces a column of True/False. Using that to index the DataFrame keeps only the True rows. This is called a boolean mask, and it is the pandas move you will use most.

cell
is_nonsense = df["variant_type"] == "nonsense"
df[is_nonsense]

# combine conditions with & (and), | (or), ~ (not) and wrap each one in parentheses
df[(df["variant_type"] == "missense") & (df["replicate"] == 1)]

# membership and text tests
df[df["variant_type"].isin(["nonsense", "synonymous"])]
df[df["variant"].str.endswith("Arg")]

# the same filter, written as a readable string
df.query("variant_type == 'missense' and replicate == 1")
and versus &

Writing df[(a) and (b)] raises ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. Python's and wants one yes/no, but you gave it a whole column of them. Use &, and keep the parentheses; without them, the operators bind in an order you did not intend.

Select by position or label

cell
df.loc[0:2, ["variant", "bin1_count"]]   # by label: rows 0 to 2 (inclusive!), named columns
df.iloc[0:2, 0:2]                         # by position: rows 0 and 1 (stop excluded), first two columns
Read the docs like a map

Open the page for DataFrame.query. Read the one-line summary, then Parameters, then jump to Examples. You do not have to understand all of it. In a notebook, put the cursor inside a function's brackets and press Shift+Tab to see the same text in place.

★

First star

How many rows are missense and from replicate 2?

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Two conditions joined with &, each in parentheses. Then count rows with len(...) or .shape[0].

one way to get it
sub = df[(df["variant_type"] == "missense") & (df["replicate"] == 2)]
print(len(sub))
★

Second star

Add up every count in the four bin*_count columns across the whole table. What is the grand total of reads?

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Select the four columns as a list, then .sum() sums each column. A second .sum() adds those four numbers together.

one way to get it
bins = ["bin1_count", "bin2_count", "bin3_count", "bin4_count"]
print(df[bins].sum().sum())
Stage 4

Score Falls: new columns, groups and pivots

★★

You will turn raw counts into one number per row, summarise it per variant, and line up replicates side by side. About 55 minutes.

Raw counts are hard to compare: one row has 20 reads, another has 700. A common fix is a weighted average of the bins. Give bin 1 weight 1, bin 2 weight 2, and so on. A row with all its reads in bin 1 scores 1, all in bin 4 scores 4, and anything between lands in between.

the formula
score = (1*bin1 + 2*bin2 + 3*bin3 + 4*bin4) / total_reads

Make new columns without loops

pandas works on whole columns at once. That is called vectorised code. It is shorter, easier to read, and much faster than looping over rows.

cell
bins = ["bin1_count", "bin2_count", "bin3_count", "bin4_count"]

df["total_reads"] = df[bins].sum(axis=1)                   # axis=1: add across the columns of each row
df["score"] = (df[bins] * [1, 2, 3, 4]).sum(axis=1) / df["total_reads"]
df[["variant", "replicate", "total_reads", "score"]].round(3)
What is axis?

axis=0 means "down the rows" (one answer per column). axis=1 means "across the columns" (one answer per row). If you get a result with the wrong shape, check the axis first.

Sort and rename

cell
df.sort_values("score")                       # smallest first
df.sort_values("score", ascending=False)
df.rename(columns={"score": "bin_score"})

Summarise by group

groupby splits the table by a column, applies a summary to each piece, and glues the answers back together: split, apply, combine.

cell
df.groupby("variant_type")["score"].mean()

# several summaries at once, with names you choose
per_variant = df.groupby("variant").agg(
    mean_score=("score", "mean"),
    reads=("total_reads", "sum"),
    n_rows=("score", "size"),
).reset_index()
per_variant.sort_values("mean_score")

Pivot: one row per variant, one column per replicate

cell
wide = df.pivot(index="variant", columns="replicate", values="score")
wide                       # columns are named 1 and 2
wide[1].corr(wide[2])      # how well do the replicates agree?
cell
wide["diff"] = (wide[1] - wide[2]).abs()
wide.sort_values("diff", ascending=False)
A mean can hide the story

Two variants can have the same average score for completely different reasons. A quick look at the raw bins shows it:

cell (no star for this one)
pick = df[(df["replicate"] == 1) & df["variant"].isin(["p.Ile40Asn", "p.Gly46Arg"])]
frac = pick[bins].div(pick["total_reads"], axis=0)   # each row now sums to 1
frac.index = pick["variant"]
frac.T.plot.bar()                                      # bins on x, one colour per variant

p.Ile40Asn piles up in the middle bins. p.Gly46Arg splits between the lowest and highest. Same average, different shapes. Stage 9 is all about plots that expose this.

Look at your pivot table before trusting it

If one variant's replicates disagree wildly, ask why before averaging them. The answer is sometimes in a column you already have.

★

First star

What is the mean score of the WT rows (both replicates), to 2 decimal places?

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Filter to rows where variant == "WT" and take .mean() of the score column.

one way to get it
print(df[df["variant"] == "WT"]["score"].mean().round(2))
★

Second star

Pivot the scores so replicates sit side by side, and take the absolute difference between replicate 1 and 2 for each variant. Which variant has the largest disagreement? Write its name exactly as it appears.

Stuck? Nudge and solution

Use the pivot and diff code above, then idxmax() on the diff column, or sort descending and read the top row. Then look at that variant's total_reads and ask whether you trust it.

one way to get it
wide = df.pivot(index="variant", columns="replicate", values="score")
wide["diff"] = (wide[1] - wide[2]).abs()
print(wide["diff"].idxmax())
Stage 5

Function Forge: write it once, reuse it forever

★★

You will turn working notebook code into a documented function, learn the habits that make it safe to reuse, and test it. About 50 minutes.

In Stage 4 you computed scores for the whole table. Now imagine a collaborator wants a different weighting, or you want to ignore rows with too few reads, or you need the same calculation for next month's dataset. Copy and paste works exactly once. The second time you paste, the two copies start to differ, and you forget which one you trust.

The rule of two

The second time you copy a block of code, turn it into a function instead. A function is a named, reusable recipe: you fix a bug in one place, and every use of it gets the fix.

Anatomy of a function

cell
BINS = ["bin1_count", "bin2_count", "bin3_count", "bin4_count"]


def add_scores(df, weights=(1, 2, 3, 4), min_reads=0):
    """Add total_reads and a weighted-average bin score.

    score = sum(weight_i * count_i) / total_reads, so 1 means every read
    is in bin 1 (lowest signal) and 4 means every read is in bin 4.

    Rows with fewer than `min_reads` total reads get score = NaN, because
    a number built from 20 reads is not one we should trust.

    Returns a new DataFrame; the input is left unchanged.
    """
    out = df.copy()
    out["total_reads"] = out[BINS].sum(axis=1)
    out["score"] = (out[BINS] * list(weights)).sum(axis=1) / out["total_reads"]
    out.loc[out["total_reads"] < min_reads, "score"] = float("nan")
    return out
  • def name(parameters): starts the recipe. Parameters with = have defaults, so callers only mention what they want to change.

  • return hands the result back. A function with no return gives back None, a classic cause of "why is my variable empty?".
  • df.copy() means the function works on its own copy and never changes the caller's table behind their back.

"""Reusable helpers for the variant-abundance analysis."""

BINS = ["bin1_count", "bin2_count", "bin3_count", "bin4_count"]


def add_scores(df, weights=(1, 2, 3, 4), min_reads=0):
    """Add total_reads and a weighted-average bin score.

    score = sum(weight_i * count_i) / total_reads. Rows with fewer than
    `min_reads` total reads get score = NaN. Returns a new DataFrame.
    """
    out = df.copy()
    out["total_reads"] = out[BINS].sum(axis=1)
    out["score"] = (out[BINS] * list(weights)).sum(axis=1) / out["total_reads"]
    out.loc[out["total_reads"] < min_reads, "score"] = float("nan")
    return out

The variant name packs three facts into one string. To summarise by position later, you need them as separate columns. A regular expression (regex) describes a text pattern; .str.extract pulls out the parts:

def parse_hgvs(df, column="hgvs_pro"):
    """Split names like 'p.Asn12Ile' into ref, position and alt columns.

    ref = 'Asn', position = 12 (nullable integer), alt = 'Ile'.
    Synonymous names like 'p.Asn12=' get alt = '='. Anything that does not
    match (for example the wild-type row '_wt') gets missing values.
    """
    pattern = r"^p\.(?P<ref>[A-Za-z]{3})(?P<position>\d+)(?P<alt>[A-Za-z]{3}|=)$"
    parts = df[column].str.extract(pattern)
    out = df.copy()
    out["ref"] = parts["ref"]
    out["position"] = pd.to_numeric(parts["position"]).astype("Int64")
    out["alt"] = parts["alt"]
    return out

def label_regions(df, regions, position_column="position"):
    """Add a 'region' column from a table with region, start and end columns.

    Positions outside every region are labelled 'other'; rows without a
    position are labelled 'no_position'.
    """
    def find(position):
        if pd.isna(position):
            return "no_position"
        for r in regions.itertuples():
            if r.start <= position <= r.end:
                return r.region
        return "other"

    out = df.copy()
    out["region"] = out[position_column].map(find)
    return out

Correlation is a number; the plot is the check

A correlation coefficient can look strong because of one cluster, or weak because the relationship is curved. Always look at the scatter that goes with it. Spearman (used above) compares ranks, so it is robust to outliers and to curved but steadily rising relationships.

Make the heatmap readable
  • Fix vmin/vmax so colours mean the same thing across plots.
  • Order the rows meaningfully (here by chemical similarity) instead of alphabetically.
  • Use a perceptually even colormap like viridis; avoid rainbow maps that invent edges.
  • Show missing cells honestly, in grey, rather than as zero.

Plot hygiene checklist

  • Axis labels with units; a title that states the finding, not just the variables.
  • Same colour = same category in every figure.
  • Text readable at the size it will be printed (14 to 16 pt at final size is a good aim).
  • Save from code, with a descriptive filename, into results/figures/.
  • Show the raw data points where you can; summaries alone hide too much.

Second star

Cut the sequence into windows of 10 positions: window = position // 10 * 10, so positions 120 to 129 form window 120. Among windows that contain at least 30 missense variants, which window has the lowest mean missense score? Answer with the window's starting number.

Stage 11

The Summit: does your conclusion survive a different rule?

★★

A result is only as solid as the choices behind it. You will change one rule, measure how much the answer moves, and package everything so anyone can re-run it. About 60 minutes.

Every analysis contains judgement calls: which rows to keep, how to score, where to cut. A trustworthy analysis shows how much the answer depends on them. Take one call you have already made implicitly: should we trust variants that were measured in only a couple of experiments?

Turn the rule into a dial

cell
def summarise(df, region="phosphatase_domain", min_expts=None):
    """Count and mean of missense scores in one region.

    min_expts: keep only variants measured in at least this many experiments
    (None keeps everything).
    """
    keep = (df["record_type"] == "missense") & (df["region"] == region)
    if min_expts is not None:
        keep &= df["expts"] >= min_expts
    return df.loc[keep, "score"].agg(["count", "mean"])

summarise(df), summarise(df, min_expts=3)

Now sweep the dial and look at the whole curve, not one cherry-picked value:

sweep = pd.DataFrame(rows)
sweep.round(3)

If the mean barely moves while the count falls, the conclusion is robust to this rule. If it swings, say so in your write-up. Either answer is a result.

This is the heart of reproducible research

Readers should be able to change the dial themselves. A function with a documented parameter lets them. A hand-edited spreadsheet does not.

After the summit

Taking your work to the HPC cluster

What this guide was for, when a laptop stops being enough, and how to move the same project onto the cluster. No stars here, just a map.

What this guide was really for

Your laptop is where you learn and where you develop. Data is small, feedback is instant, and a mistake costs seconds. Everything in the twelve stages was practice for the habits that make a cluster usable later:

Habit you builtWhy the cluster needs it
Isolated environment plus environment.ymlYou rebuild the exact same Python on the cluster in one command.
Scripts like src/make_figures.pyA cluster job runs a script, not a notebook you click through.
Relative paths from a project rootThe same code runs in a different folder on a different machine.
Functions with parametersOne script can process any sample or setting you hand it.
Raw data never edited, results regeneratedJobs can be re-run safely, and you always know where an output came from.
Reading the last line of an errorFailed jobs leave you a log file full of tracebacks. You already know how to read one.

When do you actually need HPC?

Not for this dataset: four thousand rows fit on any laptop. Develop small, then scale up when one of these happens:

  • Memory: you hit MemoryError, or your laptop starts crawling because the data does not fit in RAM.
  • Time: one run takes hours, or you need to repeat it for many samples or many parameter settings.
  • Hardware: you need many cores at once, or a GPU.
Never run heavy work on a login node

When you log in, you land on a shared machine used by everyone to edit files and submit jobs. Anything big belongs in a job that the scheduler (Slurm) places on a compute node. Start with an interactive job to try things, and a batch job once it works.

The same project, on the cluster

  1. Get access. Request an account and read how resources are allocated: getting an account and requesting resources.
  2. Log in. Use a terminal (SSH) or the browser portal (Open OnDemand). OnDemand also offers Python and Jupyter sessions if you want a notebook on a compute node.
  3. Bring your code. Put the project in a Git repository on your laptop, then git clone it on the cluster. Code travels through Git; it keeps a history and avoids "which copy is newest?".
  4. Bring your data. Large files go through a transfer tool, not Git. See file transfer (Globus is the usual choice) and the file systems page to decide where files should live. Big temporary files belong in scratch.
  5. Rebuild the environment. Load conda or Python the way the Python page describes, then recreate yours: conda env create -f environment.yml. This is why you froze it in Stage 6.
  6. Test on a small slice. Ask for a short interactive job, run your script on a few rows, and fix errors where you can see them.
  7. Submit a batch job. Write a short job script and hand it to Slurm (batch jobs).
  8. Check, then copy results home. Read the log, confirm the outputs look right, and copy results/ back to your laptop for figures and writing.

A job script

A batch script is a shell script with #SBATCH lines that tell Slurm what to reserve. The names of clusters and partitions, and sensible memory and time requests, are specific to your group; copy real values from the manual rather than from this sketch.

run_make_figures.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=make-figures
#SBATCH --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME        # placeholder: copy real values from the manual
#SBATCH --partition=PARTITION_NAME    # placeholder
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out       # %x = job name, %j = job id

# 1. make the same Python the same way you did on your laptop
#    (how to load conda or Python on the cluster is on the manual's Python page)
conda activate pandas-quest

# 2. run from the project root so relative paths behave
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

# 3. run the script, not a notebook
python src/make_figures.py

Submit it and keep an eye on it:

terminal on the cluster
mkdir -p logs
sbatch run_make_figures.sh     # prints: Submitted batch job 12345678
squeue --me                    # what is queued or running
sacct -j 12345678              # what happened, after it finishes
scancel 12345678               # stop it
Reading a failed job

The log file in logs/ is your traceback. Open it and go to the bottom, exactly like Stage 2. A job killed for time or memory says so: ask for a little more of what ran out, not ten times more. Smaller requests usually start sooner.

Habits that make cluster work painless

  • Develop small, run big. Add a small slice or a --sample option to your script so you can test in seconds.
  • Many similar tasks? Do not write a loop in one long job; use a job array so each sample runs on its own.
  • Keep sessions alive. tmux and nohup let long-running work survive a dropped connection.
  • Edit comfortably. VS Code can work on cluster files directly: see the VS Code page.
  • Record what you ran. Commit the job script, the environment.yml and the README. Next month, they are your memory.
  • Stuck? Check Common Problems and the main user manual, then ask the support team with the job ID and the last lines of the log.

Request an account and read how resources are allocated: getting an account and requesting resources.Log in. Use a terminal (SSH) or the browser portal (Open OnDemand). OnDemand also offers Python and Jupyter sessions if you want a notebook on a compute node.Bring your code. Put the project in a Git repository on your laptop, then git clone it on the cluster. Code travels through Git; it keeps a history and avoids "which copy is newest?".Bring your data. Large files go through a transfer tool, not Git. See file transfer (Globus is the usual choice) and the file systems page to decide where files should live. Big temporary files belong in scratch.Rebuild the environment. Load conda or Python the way the Python page describes, then recreate yours: conda env create -f environment.yml. This is why you froze it in Stage 6.Test on a small slice. Ask for a short interactive job, run your script on a few rows, and fix errors where you can see them.Submit a batch job. Write a short job script and hand it to Slurm (batch jobs).Check, then copy results home. Read the log, confirm the outputs look right, and copy results/ back to your laptop for figures and writing.A job scriptA batch script is a shell script with #SBATCH lines that tell Slurm what to reserve. entry.title: Case #006: The Vanishing Diamond
entry.content:
At Miami’s prestigious Fontainebleau Hotel charity gala, the famous “Heart of Atlantis” diamond necklace suddenly disappeared from its display.

Reading the case description these are the clues we can pick up:

  • Location: Fontainebleau Hotel
  • Famous “Heart of Atlantis” diamond necklace suddenly disappeared; Type of crime: theft

Going over the schema

There are 6 tables:

  • crime_scene:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • guest:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • attire_registry:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • guest_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in guest
  • witness_statements:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • guest_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in guest
  • final_interviews:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • guest_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in guest
  • marina_rentals:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • renter_guest_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in guest

Investigation

We start by looking through all the crime scenes where the location has Fontainebleau Hotel.

select * from crime_scene where location like '%Fontainebleau Hotel%';

The Heart of Atlantis necklace disappeared. Many guests were questioned but only two of them gave valuable clues. One of them is a really famous actor. The other one is a woman who works as a consultant for a big company and her first name ends with “an”.

New clues:

  • witness #1 is a famous actor
  • witness #2 is a woman who works as a consultant and her first name ends with ‘an’

Let us look at witness statements using the witness descriptions we just got. We can do this by using a JOIN on guest and witness_statements tables.

select witness_statements.guest_id, guest.name, witness_statements.clue from witness_statements 
join guest on witness_statements.guest_id = guest.id 
where guest.occupation like '%Actor%' or 
(guest.occupation like '%consultant%' and guest.name like '%an %');

I overheard someone say, “Meet me at the marina, dock 3. I saw someone holding an invitation ending with “-R”. He was wearing a navy suit and a white tie.

New clues:

  • Marina dock 3 is relevant
  • Invitation ending with ‘-R’ wearing a navy suit and white tie

Let’s look at marina rentals using the other clues as filters. We can use JOIN on guest, attire_registry, and marina_rentals.

select guest.id, guest.name, guest.invitation_code, attire_registry.note, 
marina_rentals.dock_number, marina_rentals.rental_date, marina_rentals.boat_name from guest 
join attire_registry on guest.id = attire_registry.guest_id 
join marina_rentals on guest.id = marina_rentals.renter_guest_id  
where attire_registry.note like '%navy suit, white tie%' and 
guest.invitation_code like '%-R';

We only get one entry. This has to be our guy. Let’s look at the final interview.

select guest.name, final_interviews.confession from guest 
join final_interviews on guest.id = final_interviews.guest_id 
where guest.id = 105;

“I was the one who took the crystal. I guess I need a lawyer now?” ~ Mike Manning

We got him. Too bad the spotlight never left the “Heart of Atlantis”.

Thank you Chris for creating SQL Noir.

entry.title: Case #005: The Silicon Sabotage
entry.content:
QuantumTech, Miami’s leading technology corporation, was about to unveil its groundbreaking microprocessor called “QuantaX.” Just hours before the reveal, the prototype was destroyed, and all research data was erased. Detectives suspect corporate espionage.

Reading the case description these are the clues we can pick up:

  • Location: QuantumTech
  • Prototype was destroyed, and all research data was erased; Type of crime: corporate espionage

Going over the schema

There are 7 tables:

  • incident_reports:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • employee_records:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • witness_statements:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • incident_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in incident_reports
    • emplotee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records
  • facility_access_logs:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • employee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records
  • computer_access_logs:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • employee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records
  • keycard_access_logs:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • employee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records
  • email_logs:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • sender_employee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records
    • recipient_employee_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in employee_records

Investigation

We start by looking through all the crime scenes where the location has QuantumTech.

select * from incident_reports where location like '%QuantumTech%';

Prototype destroyed; data erased from servers.

New clue:

  • Incident happened on April 21, 1989

Let us also look at witness statements for this crime. We can do this by using a JOIN on incident_reports and witness_statements tables.

select witness_statements.id, witness_statements.statement from witness_statements 
join incident_reports on witness_statements.incident_id = incident_reports.id 
where location like '%QuantumTech%';

I heard someone mention a server in Helsinki.

I saw someone holding a keycard marked QX- succeeded by a two-digit odd number.

New clues:

  • Server in Helsinki mentioned
  • Keycard marked QX- succeeded by a two-digit odd number

Using these clues we can find employees that access both the server and facility.

select * from employee_records 
where id in 
  (
    select employee_id from keycard_access_logs 
    where keycard_code like '%QX-0__' and 
    SUBSTR(keycard_code, -1, 1) in ('1', '3', '5', '7', '9') and 
    access_date = 19890421
) and 
id in 
  (
    select employee_id from computer_access_logs 
    where server_location = 'Helsinki' and 
    access_date = 19890421
);
id employee_name department occupation
99 Elizabeth Gordon Engineering Solutions Architect

Only one name pops up. Let’s take a look at the email logs either to or from this person.

select * from email_logs 
where sender_employee_id = 99 or 
recipient_employee_id = 99;

Just 1 email recieved where the sender employee id is 263. Let’s follow this trail.

select * from email_logs 
where sender_employee_id = 263 or 
recipient_employee_id = 263;

L’s schedule puts her close enough, but we need her inside F18 before 9. Trigger a minor alert or routine checkup to send her in by 8:30. Make sure she logs the visit. That part matters.

Unlock 18 quietly by 9. He’ll use his own credentials to access it shortly after L leaves. No questions. Just ensure the timing lines up. The trail will lead exactly where it needs to.

Reading the first email it looks like someone is trying to frame Elizabeth Gordon. The send email will help us get to the actual culprit. Let’s look at facility logs for facility 18.

select * from facility_access_logs where facility_name = 'Facility 18';

Only two people accessed this facility in the morning. Elizabeth and an employee with id 297. That must be our guy.

select * from employee_records where id = 297;

Hristo Bogoev, Principal Engineer

We got him. At QuantumTech, the real glitch was human.

Thank you Chris for creating SQL Noir.

entry.title: Case #004: The Midnight Masquerade Murder
entry.content:
On October 31, 1987, at a Coconut Grove mansion masked ball, Leonard Pierce was found dead in the garden.

Reading the case description these are the clues we can pick up:

  • Location: Coconut Grove mansion
  • Date: October 31, 1987
  • Leonard Pierce was found dead; Type of crime: murder

Going over the schema

There are 9 tables:

  • crime_scene:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • person:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • witness_statements:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • crime_scene_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in crime_scene
    • witness_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • final_interviews:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • vehicle_registry:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • catering_orders:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • phone_records:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • caller_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
    • recipient_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • hotel_checkins:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • surveillance_records:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • hotel_checkin_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in hotel_checkins

Investigation

We start by looking through all the crime scenes where the location has Coconut Grove and date is October 31, 1987.

select * from crime_scene where date = 19871031 and location like '%Coconut Grove%';

During a masked ball, a body was found in the garden. Witnesses mentioned a hotel booking and suspicious phone activity.

Let us also look at witness statements for this crime. We can do this by using a JOIN on crime_scene and witness_statements tables.

select witness_statements.witness_id, witness_statements.clue from witness_statements 
join crime_scene on witness_statements.crime_scene_id = crime_scene.id 
where crime_scene.date = 19871031 and 
crime_scene.location like '%Coconut Grove%';

I overheard a booking at The Grand Regency.

I noticed someone at the front desk discussing Room 707 for a reservation made yesterday.

New clues:

  • Hotel booking at The Grand Regency
  • Room 707 booked on October 30, 1987

We look into all the surveillance records for hotel checkins at The Grand Regency for room 707 on October 30, 1987.

select surveillance_records.id, surveillance_records.hotel_checkin_id, 
surveillance_records.note from surveillance_records 
join hotel_checkins on surveillance_records.hotel_checkin_id = hotel_checkins.id
where hotel_checkins.hotel_name = 'The Grand Regency' and 
hotel_checkins.room_number = 707 and
hotel_checkins.check_in_date = 19871030 and
surveillance_records.note is not NULL;
hotel_checkin_id note
119 Subject was overheard yelling on a phone: “Did you kill him?”

We can look at hotel checkins for id 119 and see which person checked in.

select * from hotel_checkins where id = 119;
id person_id hotel_name check_in_date room_number
119 11 The Grand Regency 19871030 707

We now look into the phone records for person id 11. (Query below also looks at phone records for person id 58 as they are the recipient of the call)

select * from phone_records where caller_id in (11, 58) or recipient_id in (11, 58);

“Why did you kill him, bro? You should have left the carpenter do it himself!”

“I will do it. Only if you give me that nice Lambo of yours.”

New clues:

  • Suspect maybe be a carpenter
  • Suspect owns a Lamborghini

We can use JOIN on person and vehicle_registry to find our suspect.

select * from vehicle_registry 
join person on person.id = vehicle_registry.person_id 
where car_make = 'Lamborghini' and 
person.occupation like 'carpenter';

Marco Santos is the only name which pops up. Let us look at final interview for this person.

select * from final_interviews
where person_id = 97;

“I ordered the hit. It was me. You caught me.” ~ Marco Santos

We got him. The mask slipped.

Thank you Chris for creating SQL Noir.

entry.title: Case #003: The Miami Marina Murder
entry.content:
A body was found floating near the docks of Coral Bay Marina in the early hours of August 14, 1986.

Reading the case description these are the clues we can pick up:

  • Location: Coral Bay Marina
  • Date: August 14, 1986
  • Dead body was found; Type of crime: murder

Going over the schema

There are 6 tables:

  • crime_scene:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • person:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • hotel_checkins:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • confessions:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • interviews:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
  • surveillance_records:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • person_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in person
    • hotel_checkin_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in hotel_checkin

Investigation

We start by looking through all the crime scenes where the location is Coral Bay Marina and date is August 14, 1986.

select * from crime_scene where date = 19860814 and location = 'Coral Bay Marina';

The body of an unidentified man was found near the docks. Two people were seen nearby: one who lives on 300ish “Ocean Drive” and another whose first name ends with “ul” and his last name ends with “ez”.

New clues:

  • Two people seen
    • one lives on 300ish “Ocean Drive”
    • other first name ends with “ul” and his last name ends with “ez”

We now look into the person table where address has 300ish Ocean Drive or the name is of pattern *ul *ez

select * from person 
where address like '3__ %Ocean Drive%' or 
name like '%ul %ez';

The two names that pop-up are Carlos Mendez and Raul Gutierrez. We can use JOIN on person and interviews with the filters we just used.

select interviews.transcript from interviews 
join person on interviews.person_id = person.id 
where person.address like '3__ %Ocean Drive%' or 
name like '%ul %ez';

“I saw someone check into a hotel on August 13. The guy looked nervous.” “I heard someone checked into a hotel with ‘Sunset’ in the name.”

New clues:

  • Suspect checked into a hotel on August 13, 1986
  • Hotel has ‘Sunset’ in its name

We can use JOIN this time on hotel_checkins table and person table where the check in date is August 13, 1986 and hotel has ‘Sunset’ in its name.

select * from hotel_checkins 
join person on hotel_checkins.person_id = person.id 
where hotel_checkins.hotel_name like '%Sunset%' and 
hotel_checkins.check_in_date = 19860813;

Well, this does not narrow down our list of suspects. We can look into the surveillance_records where the person_id is present in the hotel checkins we just looked at.

select * from surveillance_records where 
person_id in (
  select hotel_checkins.person_id from hotel_checkins 
  join person on hotel_checkins.person_id = person.id 
  where hotel_checkins.hotel_name like '%Sunset%' and 
  hotel_checkins.check_in_date = 19860813
) and suspicious_activity is not NULL;

After a little bit of grunt work we can narrow down our search to these suspects:

person_id hotel_checkin_id suspicious_activity
6 34 Spotted entering late at night
7 89 Seen arguing with an unknown person
8 2 Left suddenly at 3 AM

We can now look at confessions where person_id in [6, 7, 8]. To simplify, we JOIN confessions and person tables to directly get person name along with the confession.

select person.name, confessions.confession from confessions 
join person on person.id = confessions.person_id 
where person_id in (6,7,8);

“Alright! I did it. I was paid to make sure he never left the marina alive.” ~ Thomas Brown

We got him. The tide tried to keep the secret. But in Coral Bay, even the water talks.

entry.title: Case #002: The Stolen Sound
entry.content:
In the neon glow of 1980s Los Angeles, the West Hollywood Records store was rocked by a daring theft. A prized vinyl record, worth over $10,000, vanished during a busy evening, leaving the store owner desperate for answers. Vaguely recalling the details, you know the incident occurred on July 15, 1983, at this famous store.

Reading the case description these are the clues we can pick up:

  • Location: West Hollywood Records
  • Date: July 15, 1983
  • Vinyl record was stolen; Type of crime: theft

Going over the schema

There are 4 tables:

  • crime_scene:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • witnesses:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
    • crime_scene_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in crime_scene
  • suspects:
    • id: PRIMARY KEY
  • interviews:
    • suspect_id: FOREIGN KEY referencing id in suspects

Investigation

We start by looking through all the thefts that happened on July 15, 1983 at West Hollywood Records.

select * from crime_scene where location = 'West Hollywood Records' and type = 'theft' and date = 19830715;

With the query result we confirm that we are looking at the correct crime.

We now look into the witnesses related to this crime. We can do this by using a JOIN on crime_scene and witnesses tables on their common key, using the filters we just used.

select witnesses.id, witnesses.clue from witnesses 
join crime_scene on witnesses.crime_scene_id = crime_scene.id 
where location = 'West Hollywood Records' and 
type = 'theft' and date = 19830715;

“I saw a man wearing a red bandana rushing out of the store.” ~ witness #1

“The main thing I remember is that he had a distinctive gold watch on his wrist.” ~ witness #2

New clues:

  • Suspect was wearing a red bandana
  • Suspect had a gold watch

We have enough information on the suspect, so we look in the suspects table where the bandana color is red and accessory is a gold watch.

select * from suspects 
where bandana_color = 'red' and 
accessory = 'gold watch';

There are three suspects Tony Ramirez, Mickey Rivera, and Rico Delgado who match the description.

We can now look at the interviews for these three suspects to see who our culprit is. We will use a JOIN on suspects and interviews tables as they share a common key, using the filters we just used.

select suspect_id, transcript, name from interviews 
join suspects on suspects.id = interviews.suspect_id 
where bandana_color = 'red' and accessory = 'gold watch';

“I couldn’t help it. I snapped and took the record.” ~ Rico Delgado

We got him. Turns out the vinyl played both sides—and side B had all the evidence.

select * from crime_scene where location = 'Blue Note Lounge';

entry.title: Understanding 10x Xenium Data Analysis
entry.content:
Overview of Spatial Transcriptomics (ST)

Traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dissociates cells and profiles gene expression at single cell resolution. It is able to capture the heterogeneity within tissues and gives high resolution insight into cellular functions.

While this type of data can be used to analyze variations in gene expression, it lacks the spatial information for cells, which adds a dimension of information. Enter ‘Spatial Transcriptomics’ (ST)! After being named the Method of the year 2020[1] ST has revolutionized our ability to understand biology by capturing the spatial information. Having spatial context allows us to look deeper into cell-cell interactions, cellular niches, and various microenvironments across conditions.

Over the last few years, spatial transcriptomics technologies have advanced rapidly and each come with various advantages. Detailed table can be found here.

Overview of Xenium

Xenium is a single-cell resolution technology commercialized by 10x genomics in 2023. It uses RNA based transcripts and can target up to 5000 genes. It captures transcripts at subcellular level. 10x also has nuclear and cell membrane staining which are used for cell segmentation downstream, as compared to the default which only has nuclear staining and cells are detected based on cell-boundary expansion after nucleus segmentation[2].

A few caveots to note for xenium data are that the data generation for large number of samples for entire tissue sections is expensive. So the general practice is to build a Tissue Microarray (TMA) with 30-45 cores of 1.5mm-2mm diameter. Selecting these cores haphazardly can induce data bias as it captures a small section of the condition to be captured. So, building TMA with help of expert pathalogists is a necessary step. Ex: When it comes to studying cancer, the most interesting parts are boundaries between either tumor and immune cells or tumor and stromal cells. These regions are full of potential, allowing us to dive deeper into finding interactions and spatial structures between in such regions.

Understand 10x output files

The Xenium analyzer has numerous outputs we only need some of them to start with data analysis. Here are those files:

File Type File and Description
Cell summary cells.parquet: Cell summary file in Parquet format.
Cell-feature matrix cell_feature_matrix.h5: Cell-feature matrix file in HDF5 format.

Table 2: Xenium Onboard Analysis Output Files[3]

Getting started with data analysis

I will use the Human Lung Cancer with Xenium Multimodal Cell Segmentation data for showcase.

We can get started once Xenium_V1_humanLung_Cancer_FFPE_outs.zip is downloaded.

unzip -d data Xenium_V1_humanLung_Cancer_FFPE_outs.zip

Installing necessary libraries

pip install anndata scanpy squidpy

Loading the data as an AnnData object from raw output files

import os
import pandas as pd
import anndata as ad
import scanpy as sc
import squidpy as sq

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 250        # increase figure dpi for better quality plots

# load count matrix
adata = sc.read_10x_h5('data/cell_feature_matrix.h5')

# load cells metadata
cells = pd.read_parquet('data/cells.parquet')
cells.index = cells['cell_id']
cells.drop(['cell_id'], inplace=True, axis=1)

adata.obs = cells.copy()

# set spatial info
adata.obsm["spatial"] = adata.obs[["x_centroid", "y_centroid"]].copy().to_numpy()

adata.write_h5ad('objects/xenium_adata.h5ad')

Understanding xenium data structure

AnnData object with n_obs × n_vars = 162254 × 377
    obs: 'x_centroid', 'y_centroid', 'transcript_counts', 'control_probe_counts',
    'control_codeword_counts', 'unassigned_codeword_counts', 'deprecated_codeword_counts', 
    'total_counts', 'cell_area', 'nucleus_area'
    var: 'gene_ids', 'feature_types', 'genome'
    obsm: 'spatial'

adata.obs stores the metadata. adata.var stores information about the genes on the panel. More information on AnnData structure can be found here. x_centroid and y_xentroid are the x and y coordinates of the cells.

QC

print(f'Shape of object before filtering: {adata.shape}')

sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(adata, percent_top=None, inplace=True)

sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_counts=10)

print(f'Shape of object after filtering: {adata.shape}')

As part of quality control we drop cells with n_genes_by_counts < 10.

AnnData object with n_obs × n_vars = 154472 × 377
    obs: 'x_centroid', 'y_centroid', 'transcript_counts', 'control_probe_counts', 
    'control_codeword_counts', 'unassigned_codeword_counts', 
    'deprecated_codeword_counts', 'total_counts', 'cell_area', 'nucleus_area', 
    'n_genes_by_counts', 'log1p_n_genes_by_counts', 'log1p_total_counts', 'n_counts'
    var: 'gene_ids', 'feature_types', 'genome', 'n_cells_by_counts', 
    'mean_counts', 'log1p_mean_counts', 'pct_dropout_by_counts', 'total_counts', 'log1p_total_counts'
    obsm: 'spatial'

Shape of object before filtering: (162254, 377)
Shape of object after filtering: (154472, 377)

Referring to this paper we’ll normalize target_sum=100 and log normalize.

# Normalize total
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=100)

# Log-normalize
sc.pp.log1p(adata)

We will apply dimensionality reduction methods

# Run PCA
sc.pp.pca(adata)

# Calculate neighbors
sc.pp.neighbors(adata)

# Leiden clustering
sc.tl.leiden(adata)

# Computing UMAP
sc.tl.umap(adata)

We will plot the UMAP and color on leiden clusters using sc.pl.umap(adata, color='leiden', legend_loc='on data')

NOTE: I have merged some leiden clusters to group similar clusters together in a new column ‘clusters’

Layers of spatial data

Neighborhood enrichment

The reason for spatial data generation is having the x_centroid and y_centroid for each cell. This allows us to build a neighborhood graph.

sq.gr.spatial_neighbors(adata, radius=50, coord_type='generic') # radius in µm

By default this creates an entries ‘spatial_connectivities’ and ‘spatial_distances’ in in adata.obsp.

We can now run neighborhood enrichment to see which cells group together using:

# set seed=0 for reproducibility
sq.gr.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key='clusters', seed=0)

Using sq.pl.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key='clusters', cmap='bwr', vmin=-10, vmax=10) we can plot the neighborhood enrichment.

Neighborhood and Proximity scores

Another interesting analysis that is possible with spatial information is looking into neighborhoods at single-cell resolution. Using the method defined in Barkley et al[4].

connections = adata.obsp['spatial_connectivities'].tocsr()

def fetch_neighbors(connections, cell_id):
    row_idx = adata.obs_names.get_loc('cell_name')
    neighbor_idx = connections[row_idx].indices
    return adata.obs_names[neighbor_idx]

def get_neighborhood_score(adata, spot_id, target_column):
    """Returns neighborhood score
    Args:
    adata(anndata.AnnData): input anndata object
    spot_id(str): cell id
    target_column(str): celltype/cluster column
    """
    neighbors = fetch_neighbors(connections, spot_id)
    cluster = adata.obs.loc[neighbors+[spot_id]]
    return cluster[target_column].value_counts() / cluster[target_column].shape[0]

def get_proximity_score(adata, spot_id, target_column):
    """Returns proximity score
    Args:
    adata(anndata.AnnData): input anndata object
    spot_id(str): cell id
    target_column(str): celltype/cluster column
    """
    source = np.array(adata.obs.loc[spot_id, ['x_centroid', 'y_centroid']].values, dtype=np.float64)
    proximity = {}

    centroids = adata.obs.loc[adata.obs.index != spot_id, ['x_centroid', 'y_centroid']].values
    target_celltypes = adata.obs.loc[adata.obs.index != spot_id, target_column]

    for target_oi in np.unique(target_celltypes):
        target_idx = np.where(target_celltypes == target_oi)[0]
        target_coords = np.array(centroids[target_idx], dtype=np.float64)
        distances = np.linalg.norm(target_coords - source, axis=1)
        proximity[target_oi] = 1 / (1 + np.min(distances))
    return pd.Series(proximity)

The paper defines this for visium, the code provided here is updated to support xenium data. We can compare neighborhood and proximity scores between conditions across a cohort or compare these scores between different neighborhoods within the same core.

Lot of work ahead…

QC - filtering cells

Filtering cells using a global threshold for metrics like n_genes_by_counts or total_counts can lead to suboptimal results by discarding biologically relevant cells that appear low-quality in a global context but are consistent with their local tissue environment. This is because global thresholds ignore the inherent spatial structure of tissues, potentially confounding biological variation with technical noise. SpotSweeper[5] addresses this limitation by introducing a spatially aware quality control framework that leverages local neighborhood information to detect outliers based on a zscore.

References

[1] Marx, V. Method of the Year: spatially resolved transcriptomics. Nat Methods 18, 9–14 (2021). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-020-01033-y

[2] Xenium In Situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation: Workflow and Data Highlights. https://cdn.10xgenomics.com/image/upload/v1710785020/CG000750_XeniumInSitu_CellSegmentation_TechNote_RevA.pdf

[3] Xenium Output Files at a Glance. https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/2.0/tutorials/outputs/xoa-output-at-a-glance

[4] Barkley, D., Moncada, R., Pour, M. et al. Cancer cell states recur across tumor types and form specific interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Nat Genet 54, 1192–1201 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-022-01141-9

[5] Totty, M., Hicks, S.C. & Guo, B. SpotSweeper: spatially aware quality control for spatial transcriptomics. Nat Methods 22, 1520–1530 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-025-02713-3

entry.title: School Shootings in the US
entry.content:
Introduction

United states is one of the most diverse and multi-cultural places in the world. It is home to approximately 332 million, of which more than 25% are people under 17 years of age.

When compared to other countries, the US has a ratio of 120.5 firearms per 100 residents, up from 88 per 100 in 2011, highest among that of other countries around the world.

With increasing number of deaths among people under 17 due to gun violence, schools are eager to find ways to better protect their students. But the steps they are taking like clear bag packs(no bag packs in some cases), risk reinforcing an unhealthy culture of surveillance without actually preventing violence. With recent legislation pushing for gun control within US, we would like to answer questions based on the K-12 school shooting database.

Purpose of the project is to look into K-12 school shooting dataset and perform exploratory analysis using visualization techniques in answering potential questions that lawmakers will be interested in, and provide a factual report of these incidents and make this information easily available and understandable.

Getting a better grasp of school shootings, as challenging as it might be, is a clear priority for preventing harm and disruption for kids, staff, and families.

We would like to start with the number of K-12 schools in the US where school shooting has occurred, by year, with respect to number of victims, analyse patterns across seasons, quarters, and geographical locations.

About the Data

Source: K-12 School Shooting Database. Riedman, David (2022).

Description:

K-12 School Shooting Database is an open source database launched and managed by David Riedman in 2018.

The data consists of all incidents from 1970 to 2022 and is consistently updated. The dataset is divided in to 4 tables: Incident, Shooter, Victim, and Weapon.

We are using subsets of the incident, weapon, and shooter data tables to generate visualization and answer our questions.

Subset of indicent table has 2171 entries and 19 columns. All tables have features with missing values, this will be handled during the data analysis phase.

Incident Table

The table contains 2171 incidents from year 1970 to 2022.

Out of all the features in the incident table, analysis focuses on:

  • Measures like victims killed, wounded, and total number of victims
  • Time series data like date and quarter
  • Geographical information like state

Weapon Table

The original data containted a lot of empty values in the Weapon_Type column. We filled this with label unknown.

Shooter Table

The Age column in this table consists of string data, like: Adult and integer data like, 17. While data cleaning, these values were grouped into the following bins:

  • 0-12
  • 13-17
  • 18-21
  • 22-30
  • 31-50
  • 50+

The missing values in the gender column were set to unknown.

More Frequent

In the last decade, school schootings have become a frequent occuring and have been in the news regularly. This motivated us to begin our exploratory data analysis with a time series of the number of incidents in last 50 years in the US to understand how much things have changed. We used the incident table which has shooting incident records from 1970 till now.

We notice a rising trend in the number of shootings over the years which is almost 1200% increase in five decades. Where in during the 70s the yearly shooting occurrence was as low as 20, to the current time where it is almost 260 yearly. We notice a jump in the number of incidents after 2015 where it has increased almost 4 times.

…and Deadlier

We focus on the incidents in the 21st century and look at how the number of injuries and deaths has changed over the years. We use a stacked bar chart to better show both number of injuries and deaths in a year. From the graph above we can see an overview of the injuries and deaths ratio, where injuries are more than deaths however we notice that the death to injury ratio was higher in 2012 compared to the rest of the years. Looking at the data of 2012, the Sandy Hook Elementary School incident led to over 25 deaths and is more likely to have skewed the ratio.

Looking at the last 5 years, we see not only the number of incidents which has gone up, but also the number of deaths have increased.

Is it the same for everywhere?

Now lets see the state-wise spread of indicidents over the years. To visualize this we used a spike map. Here the length of the spike shows the number of total shooting incidents. As we can observe states like California, Texas, Florida have highest number of incidents followed by Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York.

On paper these states can also be classified highly populated states, so one might believe thats the reason for the high incident count. California is the most populated state followed by Texas, Florida, New York. These states rank in the top 10 states in terms of population. But, when we look ar population density, these states fall down rank. New Jersey which ranks 2nd in population density has very less shooting incidents (21 incidents) as compared to its neighbour New York (83 incidents). So high population cannot be the sole factor for the incident counts across the states.

Since, we cant generalize the occurences of incidents across all states, we delve further and look at the spread of incidents for each state across the timespan from 1970 to 2022. We can use a heatmap to visualize as it help compare all the states with each other using a sequential color scale.

As we notice, this visualization is highly similar to the cumulative incident distribution over the years we see initially. There seems to a sharp increase in number of incidents after 2015 across most of the states, denoted by a orange to dark-red shades in the right side of the visualization. Large number of white spaces in heatmap signifies that there is little to no incidents for majortiy of the states for large number of years.

This motivates us to understand recent trends inorder to correlate with current state laws. Hence we shift our focus only to incident occurence after the year 2000. Interesting patterns arise when we inspect state-wise breakdown of data from year 2000. States like California, Texas, Illinois, Florida, Pittsburgh, Ohio has seen higher incidents when compared to rest of the country, with California topping the list five times over the last 6 years. Average number of incidents across the top 5 states over the last 22 years seems to over 7. Sadly, there has been only 15 occurences where the top 5 states didnt have a single incident for an entire year over the last 22 years. Illinois has also the highest number of incidents in the recent years, which motivates us further to focus on this group of states.

If we look at the other end of the spectrum, States like Hawaii, Idaho, North Dakota, US Virgin Islands, West Virginia has low incident count with an average incident occurence of 3.8 per years over the last 22 years. Hence, we decide to compare on these two groups of state in our analysis further.

What weapons are the most common?

States with highest number of incidents

States with lowest number of incidents

Taking a look at the distribution of weapons used in states with the highest and the lowest number of incidents after the year 2000 and dig deeper by looking into the state gun laws. We use a pie chart to visualize this information between the two groups of interest.

Looking at the visualization, handguns, followed by rifles are the top 2 types of weapons used across states with the highest incidents. Interestingly, rifles are not involved in states with lower number of incidents.

While there are one or two incidents where a rifle or multiple rifles were used, the number of casualties in these case is extremely high. Looking at the visualization below, we can see this in the state of Texas, while there was only one incident where multiple rifles were used, the number of deaths in that event contributes nearly to a quarter of the total deaths in the state. We see similiar cases in other states with higher number of incidents, like California and Florida.

Victims Killed vs Weapon Used

How old?

After looking at what weapons are used, we now look into who uses them. To get a closer look, the gender of the shooters and to which age group they belong to are visualized. We grouped the ages into six categories: 0-12, 13-17, 18-21, 22-30, 31-50, and 50+ years.

It is highly evident that majority of the shooters were male. The age category of 13-17 cause most number of incidents followed by 18-21 age category. Even among the female gender, we observe age category of 13-17 contribute the highest to the total number of incidents.

This raises concern for school authorities. There can be some psychological reason for that to happen. Our dataset contained two possible reasons namely Domestic Abuse or Bullying. We found these incidents to be not related to them. No domestic violence was found for 1892 incidents out of the total incidents, while 1771 indicated no bullying. So there can be some other reasons, which are not present in our dataset.

Gun Laws

To make sense of access to the weapons used, we refer to gun laws in states with the highest and lowest incidents.

All states in top 5 except for California and Illinois have little to no restrictions on sales of weapon type, magazine size, and necessity of background checks. Texas is the only state to have campus carry. Campus carry is allows carrying of guns in parking lots, outdoor walkways on campus, and concealed carry in campus buildings.

While some states with least amount of incidents have little to no restrictions, their low number of incidents can be because of extremely low population in these states. States like Hawaii, Idaho, and West Virginia have population less than 2 million, where as North Dakota has population of about 750k and the US Virgin Islands have the least population, around 110k.

In addition to having low population, the state of Hawaii also has stricter gun laws.

Do we see a pattern?

To uncover seasonality trends, we were interested into seeing what quarter of the year has the most number of incidents. For this, we use a line chart highlighting the last 5 years and plotting number of incidents over quarters.

We observed a couple of things:

  • There has been a tremendous increase in number of incidents in last 5 years.
  • All years have higher number of incidents in Fall.

Conclusion

While most states have an age limit of 18 to purchase weapons, We observed that the shooters aged 13-17 contribute the highest. Since they can’t legally buy a weapon, one possible measure is to increase safe keeping of guns among adults. Gun safe keeping programs can also be mandated when one purchases a weapon.

In addition to this, increasing the age limit for purchasing weapons to 21 will benefit, as the age range 18-21 has the 2nd highest amount of shooters.

States with no laws restricting access to rifles leads to incidents with higher casualties. Restricting access to automatic rifles, in all states will significantly reduce the number of fatalities.

Since there are a lot of unknowns in the weapon type feature of the weapons’ table, reducing this could help us uncover patterns.

Looking into the possibility of psychological reasons, we analysed two features from the incident table, namely Domestic Abuse and Bullied. No domestice violence was found for 87% of 2171 total incidents, while 81% indicated no bullying. So there can be many other factors that can be the causes. States should focus on helping schools build a safe space for students to open up about their problems and anxieties and take necessary steps to help them.

These incidents are rising at an alarming rate and have happened in every part of the country. From our analysis, we infer that,there is no single reason which cause school shootings and we believe there cannot be any one single solution that is going to address this problem.

Team: Atharva Bhagwat, Danna Alamer, Karthik Udhayakumar, Shreeraj Pawar
